claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets stem primarily from composition-induced variations in local lattice distortion.
Short-range-order variations are a primary cause of deformation and failure differences among these alloys.
Local lattice distortion and short-range order alter dislocation mobility.
Local lattice distortion and short-range order alter interactions among slip systems.
Changes in dislocation mobility and slip-system interactions produce differences in yield strength, work hardening, and ductility.
Removing one or two constituents from the quinary alloy changes the extent and spatial distribution of local lattice distortion.
Composition changes alter dislocation pinning and slip behavior through their effects on lattice distortion.
Larger local lattice distortions can increase lattice friction.
Increased lattice friction may enhance yield strength.
Increased lattice friction may enhance work hardening.
Reduced lattice distortion may lower strength.
Reduced lattice distortion may increase ductility.
Selected quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit yield-strength and ductility differences relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Yield strength, work-hardening rate, and ductility will correlate with measured lattice distortion and short-range order across the alloy series.
Alloys with optimized distortion levels may have higher yield strength and work-hardening rates than the quinary baseline.
Alloys with substantially reduced distortion may be softer and more ductile than the quinary baseline.
The proposed mechanism is limited to identically processed, single-phase FCC alloys tested at room temperature under standardized strain-rate conditions.
XRD peak broadening and TEM imaging can provide quantitative measures of local lattice distortion and indicators of short-range ordering in these alloys.
